Lucelle
loo-SELL
n. (the Jura Cistercian abbey of 1123, mother of Salem, Frienisberg, Pairis and Kaisheim)
French Lucelle, from Latin Lucis Cella, the cell of light, or from Lutzel, little.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lucelle, Lützel in German, lies in a narrow valley of the Jura exactly on what is now the boundary between France and Switzerland. Founded in 1123 and affiliated to Morimond in 1124, it became one of the most fertile mother houses in the order, sending colonies to Salem, Pairis, Frienisberg, Kaisheim, Bellelay, Neuburg and others, so that much of the Cistercian presence in Alsace, Swabia and the Swiss plateau descends from this one cramped valley. It was suppressed at the French Revolution and almost nothing of the abbey remains above ground. This dictionary records Lucelle for the disproportion between a small place and a long line, and for its Latin name, the cell of light. Scripture is consistent that light is given to be put where it will be seen, “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel” (Mat 5:15), and that the people of God are the ones carrying it, “Ye are the light of the world” (Mat 5:14). The light itself is not ours, “I am the light of the world” (Joh 8:12), and the direction of travel is settled, “the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines light as that which makes objects visible; a cell as a small close apartment; a candle as a light made of tallow or wax; to kindle as to set on fire; and a colony as a company transplanted from a parent state.

expand to see more

LIGHT, n. That ethereal agent or matter which makes objects perceptible to the sense of seeing; also, illumination of mind; instruction; knowledge.

CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; also, a small cave or hollow place; the hut of a hermit.

CANDLE, n. A long but small cylindrical body of tallow, wax or spermaceti, containing a wick composed of linen or cotton threads.

KINDLE, v.t. To set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to light; as, to kindle a fire.

COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:15 — "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house."

Mat 5:14 — "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."

Joh 8:12 — "Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life."

Pro 4:18 — "But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day."

Modern Corruption

Jura abbey of 1123, the cell of light: a cramped valley that sent colonies across Alsace, Swabia and Switzerland, and now has almost nothing standing.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one in the name. A cell of light is a contradiction unless the light is meant to leave, and the Lord makes exactly that point about the absurdity of hiding it, “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick” (Mat 5:15). Lucelle's significance lies entirely in what it sent out.

The second thing is the order of the two claims. Christ tells his people they are the light of the world, “Ye are the light of the world” (Mat 5:14), and also says of himself that he is, “I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness” (Joh 8:12). The two are not in competition; one is the source and the other the reflector, and a reflector that forgets which it is goes out. The direction of a genuine light is given plainly, “that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek luchnos (G3088), a lamp; Greek phos (G5457), light; Greek modios (G3426), a bushel; Hebrew 'or (H216), light; Hebrew nogahh (H5051), brightness.

expand to see more

Greek luchnos (G3088) — a lamp, lit to be set up; “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel”, Matthew 5:15.

Greek phos (G5457) — light, said of his people; “Ye are the light of the world”, Matthew 5:14.

Greek skotia (G4653) — darkness, what the follower escapes; “he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness”, John 8:12.

Hebrew 'orach (H734) — a path, the way of the just; “the path of the just is as the shining light”, Proverbs 4:18.

Hebrew nogahh (H5051) — brightness, increasing to full day; “that shineth more and more unto the perfect day”, Proverbs 4:18.

Usage

"“Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel” (Mat 5:15) — the absurdity the abbey's name risks."

"“I am the light of the world” (Joh 8:12) — the source, as against the reflector."

"“that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18) — the direction of a real light."
